prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice atomic clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the lattice clock third, and I have moved the clock to the top after reading the other seven ballots. It is the one entry on which attribution, maturity and measurement quality all line up. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating thousands of atoms, and Ye's group pushed the systematic uncertainty and stability to about 1e-18. Several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) now reproduce that performance and compare clocks across sites, which is exactly the independent confirmation I ask of any claimed result. It is a new measurement capability that opens fundamental tests (gravitational redshift over millimetres, constancy of constants, relativistic geodesy) and underlies the roadmap to a redefinition of the second. It was ranked by seven of eight members and in the top three by four, so it also gives the Chair something close to a consensus basis. As an instrument builder I recognise how much calibration and systematics control sits behind a number like 1e-18.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the redefinition of the SI second is still pending, so one can argue for waiting until the field's most visible deliverable has landed. There is also overlap with earlier prizes: Ye shared the 2005 prize for frequency combs and Wineland's ion-clock work was recognised in 2012, so a reader could see the lattice clock as an incremental step in a line already rewarded. Finally, AMO precision measurement is outside my own expertise, and the Sr-lattice priority history between the Tokyo and JILA groups would need expert reports to confirm that Katori and Ye are the right and sufficient pair.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest case of precision atomic physics opening new fundamental tests, with a natural two-person credit, while admitting she does not fully know the Sr-lattice priority history between groups.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the natural pair, and her caveat is the right one. I would not treat the priority question as closed on our say-so; an expert report should check whether other early Sr lattice-clock work (for example at SYRTE, PTB or NIST) deserves credit before we fix the names. My expectation is that Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy record still stand, but I want that verified, not assumed.

responses.point: Mehlig puts topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a clean general mechanism, but notes that the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions makes the novelty case more delicate, and he ranks the clock only fourth because redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I accept that topological insulators are a deep idea and I defer to him and Eriksson on the condensed-matter merit. My difficulty is attribution: the credited list has four names for a three-person limit, and the BHZ proposal, Mele and the 3D ARPES strand cannot all be accommodated, so any trio is a visible compromise. On his point about waiting for the redefinition, I would say the prize is for the clocks' demonstrated performance, which is already independently confirmed, not for a metrological decision taken by another body.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, while flagging his own conflict and risk of overweighting a field he works in.
responses.response: I respect that he flagged it, and the physics is excellent. But Kroll notes the same overlap from the other side, and I am wary of rewarding the superconducting-circuit platform again so soon after 2025. Circuit QED has fewer outside-the-field independent checks in my sense than the clocks, and I would put it behind the lattice clock for now. He also ranks the clock second, so I read us as close here.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery first as the decisive empirical confirmation of the mass mechanism, with attribution spread over ATLAS and CMS and a need for expert reports to settle the names.
responses.response: As a detector builder I agree the experimental Higgs discovery is monumental and I keep it as an alternative. My serious qualification is that the theory was recognised in 2013 and any three names from ATLAS and CMS leave out a founder; I ranked Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra, he chose Virdee over Jenni, and that disagreement among us shows how contested the allocation is. The lattice clock avoids that problem entirely.

uncertainties: Whether expert reports confirm that Katori and Ye are the right pair given the Sr-lattice priority history across RIKEN, JILA and other groups.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the SI second before recognising lattice clocks.
Whether the overlap with the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion control) prizes weakens the claim of a new prize unit.
IceCube credit among Halzen, Spiering, Karle and the AMANDA/Baikal precursors remains unsettled, so my own earlier first choice is not obviously prize-ready.
statement.conflict_note: I work in astroparticle physics and detector development (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur), which is adjacent to IceCube (B009), an alternative I list; I have no direct IceCube affiliation, but I will keep this in mind for any discussion of that ballot. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B053.
